I checked the runtimes and downstream importers. Docker Engine 23 supports normal zstd pulls without the containerd image store; the classic-store tests passed on 23.0.6/29.1.3 and failed on 20.10.24. Containerd 1.5 has a built-in decoder, and Podman 1.6.2 includes it through containers/image. Those last two are source/dependency checks, not new runtime tests. Podman's gzip push default doesn't prevent it from pulling zstd. [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/release-notes/23.0/), [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.5.0/archive/compression/compression.go), [Podman dependencies](https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/v1.6.2/go.mod), [containers/image decoder](https://github.com/containers/image/blob/v4.0.0/pkg/compression/compression.go).

The two gotchas I found are Enroot and SOCI. Enroot 3.5's actual download/cache function fails to produce the right tar from zstd input; I reproduced that with a small fixture and gzip controls. Enroot 4.0 adds zstd, but 4.2 fixes mixed-compression images, which matters when someone adds a gzip layer to our image. Pyxis uses that importer too. SOCI v0.15.0 cannot build zstd lazy-loading indexes, even though ordinary containerd unpack supports the image. [Enroot 4.0](https://github.com/NVIDIA/enroot/releases/tag/v4.0.0), [mixed-layer fix in 4.2](https://github.com/NVIDIA/enroot/releases/tag/v4.2.0), [SOCI source](https://github.com/awslabs/soci-snapshotter/blob/v0.15.0/ztoc/compression/zinfo.go).

Hub delivery and full vLLM serving already passed. I also checked the copy/build/archive paths: an added layer can create a mixed-compression image, and a mirror can re-encode it, so signing/scanning needs to cover the final delivered digest. Other OCI registries are expected to work, but I haven't run a separate cloud matrix.

I'd keep this opt-in for now. A zstd default looks reasonable if we document the supported runtime/importer versions and keep an easy-to-find gzip compatibility tag, including for SOCI users. Without that, changing the existing tag would break some downstream workflows.

Thanks for this optimization. I mapped this PR's copy site against a new fixed-cohort pure-decode trace so we have a concurrency-relevant estimate in addition to the batch-one result in the description.

Profile setup: 8 x MI355X (gfx950), TP8, BF16/MXFP4, non-speculative decode, prefix caching, 63,911-token shared prefix + 4,089-token suffix, full HIP-graph replay, and `+fused_rms_norm_gated`. The baseline was vLLM `25e1f81e1b8def93d7228a38b83348880babbe7b` with AITER `61549c5c2623316d24ce54dcf35438173cb4d95b`. The fixed-cohort pure-GPU step periods were 32.82 ms at C16 and 35.98 ms at C24.

The trace contains 93 post-attention-projection `__amd_rocclr_copyBuffer` launches per step: 69 KDA copies targeted by this PR and 24 MLA copies targeted by #50847. The complete 93-copy group costs about 0.495 ms at C16 and 0.563 ms at C24. Since all copies have the same `[batch, 7168]` BF16 shape, the 69-copy KDA share is approximately:

We've also been designing and implementing a snapshot-based sleep L3 mode for vLLM over the past few weeks. What we hit: the process held an fd open on a JIT cache lock file. The file existed at capture; the JIT stack deleted it after compilation finished. First restore passed (4.83 s, oracle matched); every later restore failed in CRIU. Same shape with compiler temp files (`/tmp/cc*.s`). Given the cross-host direction we said we want to push, we think the fix should be shaped as the first step of an attachment mechanism:

1. Capture the enumerated cache files into the artifact — path, digest, content — and write them back before CRIU restore. On the same host this makes the artifact self-healing instead of permanently dead. On a target host these files don't exist at all, so a validate-only check can never pass there; capture-and-materialize is the same code path for both.
2. For descriptors that are safe to close — lock files, mainly; the JIT stack re-locks on its next compile — closing them at the quiescence point is the cleanest fix: CRIU never records them, so the dependency is gone rather than detected later. If there's an elegant way to do this in-engine, we think it's worth doing. Fail-closed: whitelist patterns like `*.lock`, report the rest.
3. Mapped files (JIT `.so`) can't be closed; CRIU reopens them by path anyway. Pointing the cache roots (`VLLM_CACHE_ROOT`, FlashInfer, ...) into the artifact at create makes those self-contained.

I'm a colleague of @fuhefei . I read through your PR, and I noticed you have some logic around checking TCP connections — that's an area where we ran into a pitfall once with CRIU, so I wanted to give you a heads-up.

Here's the issue: while CRIU is dumping, it installs iptables/nftables rules to lock the network. If the dumpee is killed after the dump finishes, CRIU deliberately leaves those rules in place and only removes them at restore time, when it unlocks the network.

I suspect that for CRIU, "kill" means the caller intends to restore in place, while --leave-running / --leave-stopped mean the process will be migrated. And those two options also behave differently to the link-remap files.

Finally, I tried running the code in this PR — with the server startup deferred and HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 set, vLLM didn't establish any TCP connections, so I didn't see any leftover iptables rules.

So this isn't a bug report, just a heads-up. Hope it helps you avoid this pitfall.
